items.title: Earlybird: Predictive Streaming Speech Recognition in 29M Parameters
items.summary_1line: Streaming speech recognizers output a word only after the speaker has finished it, typically 90-400 ms later. For a voice agent every millisecond counts: the sooner the words are outputted, the sooner the agent can start a search or plan its reply. We present Earlybird, a 29M-par
items.editor_note: The latency angle: frames word-output delay as the cost a voice agent pays before it can start responding.

editorial.tldr: This is a topical cluster of three independent arXiv papers on speech recognition, not one unfolding event. A late-October paper ran Kroko, a 65.7M-parameter streaming Zipformer2 transducer, at 2 and 4 bits on an ESP32-P4 microcontroller with no neural accelerator, and a second argued that ASR benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance.
editorial.whats_new: Earlybird, a 29M-parameter predictive streaming recognizer, targets the 90-400 ms that streaming ASR typically waits after a speaker finishes a word before outputting it, a delay it frames as a voice-agent cost.
editorial.why_it_matters: The three papers touch separate parts of a voice-agent stack: where the recognizer can run, how soon it emits words, and whether a single-reference benchmark can score speech models that generate rather than transcribe.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat all three as single-paper claims: before changing a voice pipeline, measure your own recognizer's word-finalization delay, since that is the number Earlybird's 90-400 ms framing says to compare against.

beats.headline: A 65.7M-parameter streaming transducer runs on an ESP32-P4 in 2 and 4 bits
beats.summary: The target chip has two 400 MHz RISC-V cores, a 128-bit SIMD extension and 32 MB of PSRAM, with no neural accelerator.

beats.headline: A benchmark proposal for grounded generative speech recognition
beats.summary: The paper argues that speech language models moved ASR from transcription to general speech-to-text generation while benchmarks kept one reference transcript per utterance.

beats.headline: Earlybird predicts words early to cut streaming lag in 29M parameters
beats.summary: It starts from the observation that streaming recognizers output a word 90-400 ms after the speaker finishes it.

open_questions: What accuracy does the 2-bit and 4-bit Kroko encoder lose against the full-precision model, and does it run in real time on the ESP32-P4?
How much of the 90-400 ms output delay does Earlybird remove, and at what word-error cost when a prediction is wrong?
Do existing speech language models rank differently under a grounded generative benchmark than under single-reference WER?
Does any of the three papers ship code or weights that others can reproduce?
